faqs.q: A snake is living in my Scottsville stone foundation — what should I do?
faqs.a: Leave it alone and keep dogs away until it is identified. Most foundation snakes here are harmless black rat snakes or northern watersnakes drawn by frogs and rodents along the river, but the eastern copperhead is venomous and occurs statewide, so nobody should guess. A Commercial Nuisance Animal Permit holder can capture a non-listed snake and move it a short distance — within Scottsville's county or a neighboring one, into suitable habitat, with the release-site landowner's written permission, reported to the Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources. Listed snakes are never handled that way; they are a call to DWR.

Scottsville.wildlife_intro:
Scottsville lives with the James River in a way few Albemarle towns do — the river bends hard around downtown, floods have shaped the levee and the raised foundations, and the bottomland along the Hardware River stays wet and wooded right up to back fences. That water-first landscape drives our work here: Norway rats work the older warehouse and foundation runs near Valley Street, raccoons den in raised crawlspaces and unused chimneys after high water pushes them upland, and northern watersnakes and black rat snakes turn up in stone foundations and riverside woodpiles, where the venomous eastern copperhead — found statewide — is the snake to leave alone until it is identified.

River towns reward early action. A rat run along a stone foundation becomes a whole-block problem if the sealing waits, and a bat colony in a tall old roofline above the floodplain is far easier to exclude in late summer, after young are flying, than to deal with mid-winter. We finish Scottsville jobs by hardening the foundation vents, caps, and gutter lines the river side of town keeps testing.

Ivy.wildlife_intro:
West of Charlottesville, Ivy is foothill estate country — big wooded lots along Ivy Creek and the Mechum River, horse barns and spring houses behind the main houses, and canopy so continuous that wildlife rarely has to cross open ground to reach a roof. Groundhogs are the signature Ivy call: they burrow under barn floors, run-in sheds, and stone retaining walls, and a working burrow system can hollow out a slab edge in a single season. Barns here also hold summer bat colonies, and gray squirrels commute from the creek woods straight into attic soffits.

Because Ivy properties carry so many outbuildings, we inspect the whole parcel, not just the house — a skunk family under a spring house or starlings nesting in a barn vent will keep reseeding problems at the main roof until every structure is dealt with. The closing work in Ivy is usually a package: burrow treatment at the barn, exclusion hardware on the outbuildings, and chew-proof sealing where the house roof meets the trees.
